messages.subject: advanced.procD for single factor model?
parts:
Hi All,

Forgive the simple question, but I'd like to set up a pairwise Procrustes ANOVA using just one factor, but I can't figure out how to code it. I tried setting f2 = NULL but I get an error. Perhaps because there is no covariate? I get a significant shape~lineage effect using procD.lm, and now I would like to know which lineages are significantly different from each other. I already got an insificant shape~size*lineage result, so I figure I can leave size out. I did have a significant shape~size regression with R^2 0.15.

Thanks if someone can tell me how to set up the advanced.procD.lm model

Best,
Christy

messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] advanced.procD for single factor model?
parts:
Hi Christy,

 

If I understand your question correctly, you wish to know which lineages differ from one another in shape. That is fairly simple to do in advanced.procD.lm.  Your f1 is: shape~lineage, and f2 is ~1 (just the intercept). So, in your case you would have:

 

advanced.procD.lm(shape ~ lineage, ~ 1, groups = ~lineage, iter=999, data = gdf)

 

The help file provides other more complicated examples whose structure you could follow if you wished to incorporate size as a covariate.

 

Best,

 

Dean

Hi Mike,

Thanks for the feedback; it was and is my working assumption that the error is my fault. But I did some testing with the plethodon dataset and I can reproduce the error - here are the details...

Based on the plethodon example provided in geomorph, gdf is a geomorph dataframe that includes 4 things...
1. coords [1:12, 1:2, 1:40]
2. Csize [1:40]
3. species: factor w/2 levels (with an equal number of values to match 1:40)
4. site: factor w/2 levels  (with an equal number of values to match 1:40)

Example code from trajectory.analysis help page
data(plethodon) 
Y.gpa <- gpagen(plethodon$land)   
gdf <- geomorph.data.frame(Y.gpa, species = plethodon$species, site = plethodon$site)
TA <- trajectory.analysis(coords ~ species*site, data=gdf, iter=199)
summary(TA, angle.type = "deg")
plot(TA)

This produces a trajectory analysis.

If I make one substitution to the above dataframe, for example.

NewFactor = Factor w/4 levels  (10 levels of '1', 10 levels of '2', 10 levels of '3', 10 levels of '4' for a total of 40 values to match sample number in plethodon dataset)

gdf$species <- NewFactor

So now the gdf dataframe looks like this...
1. coords [1:12, 1:2, 1:40]
2. Csize [1:40]
3. species: factor w/4 levels (with an equal number of values to match 1:40)
4. site: factor w/2 levels  (with an equal number of values to match 1:40)

Rerun the trajectory analysis
TA <- trajectory.analysis(coords ~ species*site, data=gdf, iter=199)

ERROR: Error in array(x, c(length(x), 1L), if (!is.null(names(x))) list(names(x), : 'data' must be of a vector type, was 'NULL'

Notice no field name was changed, the only thing that was altered was the number of factors (from 2 to 4) in gdf$species.

Is my working assumption correct or?

Please advise - Cheers,
Jeremy

On Friday, September 16, 2016 at 7:33:54 AM UTC-6, Dean Adams wrote:

Hi Christy,

 

If I understand your question correctly, you wish to know which lineages differ from one another in shape. That is fairly simple to do in advanced.procD.lm.  Your f1 is: shape~lineage, and f2 is ~1 (just the intercept). So, in your case you would have:

 

advanced.procD.lm(shape ~ lineage, ~ 1, groups = ~lineage, iter=999, data = gdf)

 

The help file provides other more complicated examples whose structure you could follow if you wished to incorporate size as a covariate.

Jeremy,

trajectory,analysis is a special analysis, unlike the versatile pairwise comparisons one can do in advanced.procD.lm.  If you have a nested design, it might not be the right analysis.  If however, you feel like your sites are commensurate (maybe high-latitude versus low altitude, or lake versus stream, or something along these lines), you can create a new factor from the site factor that has representation in both species factors, and the analysis should work.

The other option in trajectory.analysis is if you have data arranged as a concatenated set, e.g., | Y1 | Y2 | Y3 | … | Yp |, for the p points of a trajectory, where Y are data matrices.  I don’t think this is what you want to do, if your data are not already arranged as such.

Good luck!
Mike
